items.title: SC rules 24-hour arrest deadline begins from detention, not formal arrest
points: New Delhi, The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the 24-hour constitutional deadline for producing an arrested person before a magistrate begins from the moment he is detained, and not from the time the police formally makes the arrest.
"The view that 24 hours begin only from the formal arrest is contrary to the constitutional mandate of Article 22 and Section 56 of the BNSS," the bench observed.
The verdict that the only period that can be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline is the time reasonably required to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.
The time spent on inquiry, investigation, search or seizure before formal arrest cannot be excluded, it added.

Article 22 provides that every person, who is arrested and detained in custody must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court.

items.title: 24-hour to produce before Magistrate starts from detention, not ‘formal arrest’: Supreme Court
points: A view of the Supreme Court of India in New Delhi.

File | Photo Credit: Sushil Kumar Verma The Supreme Court in a judgment on Thursday (November 5, 2026) held that the 24-hour period for production of an individual before a Magistrate commences from the moment of detention, and not formal arrest.

A judgment authored by a Bench headed by Justice Ujjal Bhuyan blurred the difference between detention and arrest, saying both lead to the restriction of the fundamental right to liberty of the individual.
If the period of detention extended beyond 24 hours without production before a Magistrate, the individual concerned must be released.
At the time of production, a Magistrate must record the exact date and time of detention to ensure whether 24-hour timeline was complied with.
“Article 22(2) does not sanction exclusion of the time taken for inquiry or investigation before the arresting authority could effect arrest of the detainee.
This is beyond the mandate of clause (2) of Article 22.

items.title: Cert-In issues AI security audit guidelines, sets 4-tier risk framework
points: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (Cert-In) has issued comprehensive security auditing guidelines for artificial intelligence (AI) systems that require organisations that have developed or deployed AI in India to conduct regular security assessments.
The 107-page document, titled AI Security Auditing Guidelines, also applies to organisations that handle Indian data, including foreign companies that offer AI services or tools to Indian users.
A working group at India’s national cybersecurity agency prepared the document, which was released on November 4.
For moderate-risk systems, the document prescribes an annual independent audit by an auditing organisation empanelled with Cert-In.
Cert-In emphasised that compliance requirements for high-risk and critical systems apply uniformly, with no exemptions or relaxed standards for smaller firms or startups.

The guidelines extend Cert-In’s existing rules, under which reportable incidents must be flagged within six hours and logs kept for 180 days, to AI-related incidents, and make compliance part of the audit.

items.title: Equinor shuts North Sea platform after fire
points: Norwegian energy giant Equinor has shut down production at its Visund oil and gas platform in the North Sea following a fire in an electrical switchboard room.

The incident occurred shortly before 11 am local time on Wednesday, with reports of smoke followed by flames in a room containing equipment used to control and distribute electrical power across the installation.
All 128 personnel aboard the platform were accounted for, with approximately 70 evacuated or transferred to nearby offshore installations.
Equinor spokeswoman Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk confirmed that the fire had been extinguished by mid-afternoon, although work to bring the incident fully under control continued.

According to Norwegian gas system operator Gassco, available export capacity from Visund was initially reduced to 2.5m cu m per day on Thursday before being scheduled to fall to zero for the following gas day.
Visund is located in the Tampen area of the North Sea, northeast of the Gullfaks field.
Production started in 1999, with gas exported through the Kvitebjørn pipeline to the Kollsnes processing plant.

items.title: UK moves to end new North Sea oil and gas exploration licences
points: The UK government has introduced legislation that would end new oil and gas exploration licences in the North Sea while creating a mechanism to support continued production from existing offshore developments.
The Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority’s power to issue new licences for exploring previously unlicensed oil and gas fields.

However, the legislation introduces Transitional Energy Certificates allowing companies to access additional resources in and around existing fields, including discoveries that can be developed through tiebacks to established offshore infrastructure.

The proposal forms part of the government’s North Sea Future Plan, which seeks to manage declining domestic production while supporting investment in existing infrastructure and the transition towards renewable energy.
Government figures indicate that UK oil and gas production in 2025 was approximately 75% below its historical peaks.
Ministers maintain that new exploration licensing would not reverse the basin’s long-term decline.
